source: Written 2026-10-23/24 by Claude Sonnet from our own summaries of the NC 2017 standards, and solved blind by Claude Opus (Claude Code agents, not runAi: no ai_runs rows), code-checked by lintQuestion; "checked" questions await a platform admin.

notes.NC17.4.OA.1: Grade 4 multiplicative comparison within facts and a few 2- and 3-digit products and quotients. Skills: interpreting a comparison equation, choosing an equation, find larger / smaller / how many times, additive versus multiplicative, multi-step. Wrote 69 (23 per difficulty), all whole numbers within Grade 4 multiplication facts and multi-digit by one-digit. Contexts avoid the first-pass stems; no figure needed.
notes.NC17.4.OA.3: All whole-number answers; products stay within 4-digit by 1-digit and 2-digit by 2-digit. Estimation questions state the rounding place, so each has one answer. Remainder questions say whether to round up, drop or use the remainder.
notes.NC17.4.OA.4: All numbers stay within 50 (the summary range). Prime/composite questions use numbers up to 50 only. Numbers kept within 50 for factors and primality; multiples go no higher than 100.
notes.NC17.4.NBT.1: Whole numbers up to 100,000 only; every product or quotient stays within that range. Skills (rough counts): value of a digit 4, each place ten times the place to its right 4, compare a digit in two places 4, multiply or divide by 10 5, name the place 2, explain place-value statements 4, count in place-value units 4, build a number from its places 3. Model-based items (blocks, place-value charts) are asked as written statements.
notes.NC17.4.NBT.2: Whole numbers to 100,000. Numeric questions give the numeral without commas; word forms are choice questions. Skills: words (5), numeral from words (5), expanded form (5), numeral from expanded form (5), matching forms (5), zeros as placeholders (5).
notes.NC17.4.NBT.7: Numbers are within 100,000. Comparisons are written with $>$, $=$ and $<$; number-line and place-value-chart pictures are not used.
notes.NC17.4.NBT.6: Arrays and area models are described in words (a rectangle with an area and a width). Quotients with remainders are written like "9 R 3" in choice questions only; numeric questions ask for the quotient or the remainder separately.
notes.NC17.4.NF.2: Denominators 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12 and 100 only; comparisons are written with $>$, $<$ and $=$. Models are written out in words (equal parts, a whole cut into parts). Skills (rough counts): benchmark one half 4, common denominator 4, common numerator 4, true comparison statement 2, order fractions 4, fractions in a story 5, justify a comparison 3, closest to a benchmark or between two fractions 4.
notes.NC17.4.NF.3: Denominators 2-12 (common Grade 4 set). Mixed-number answers are written 'w n/d' and may be unsimplified (e.g. 4 2/4, 6/12) so the key follows the working; equivalent forms are accepted. Choice keys that are fractions have no compute (lint rejects compute for a non-plain-number key).
notes.NC17.4.NF.6: Grade 4 decimal notation is limited to tenths and hundredths, with a few sums that pass 1 (as in 4.NF.5). Numeric answers may be given as a fraction or a decimal (for example 34/100 or 0.34). Comparing decimals and decimal addition with carrying belong to other standards and are not asked.
notes.NC17.4.NF.7: Models are described in words (a square cut into 100 or 10 equal parts, shaded columns and squares). The statement's records with >, = and < appear as true-statement choices because a bare symbol cannot be a four-option choice.
notes.NC17.4.MD.1: Questions are one-step and stay with whole numbers: larger units to smaller ones, comparisons, unit choice and estimates, and one-step problems. Converting a smaller unit to a larger one (which needs fractions or decimals) is left out as beyond the grade.
notes.NC17.4.MD.2: Only larger-to-smaller conversions with whole-number answers (m, cm, mm, km, kg, g, L, mL). Length models are written as lines of meter sticks; tables are written out.
notes.NC17.4.MD.8: A clock time is not a number, so end and start times are choice questions; numeric questions ask for minutes (or minutes past a named hour). Subtract time intervals has 7 questions because several elapsed-time stories also subtract.
notes.NC17.4.MD.3: Grade 4 area and perimeter of rectangles and rectilinear figures (composed or with a piece cut out), all with whole numbers. Rectilinear shapes are described by the rectangles that make them (no figure is referred to). Perimeter of an L-shape is not asked, as it cannot be stated fairly in words. Fixed area and fixed perimeter are asked as listing/counting rectangles with whole-number sides, comparing perimeters or areas, and finding greatest or least.
notes.NC17.4.MD.4: Line plots, bar graphs and tables are written as lists of counts (each X stands for one item); one question shows data in fourths of an inch. Collecting data is tested through the choice of question, the table and the plot, not by running a survey.
notes.NC17.4.MD.6: The protractor cannot be shown, so readings are given in words: which mark a ray crosses, and which scale starts at 0 on the first ray. Whole degrees only; no angle sums of triangles or vertical angles (later grades).
notes.NC17.4.G.2: Shapes are given by their sides and angles in words. Naming questions say "most specific name" so that rectangle, square, rhombus and parallelogram are never both defensible; a trapezoid is always described as having exactly one pair of parallel sides, and no question asks whether one kind of shape belongs inside another (that is grade 5).
notes.NC17.4.G.3: Shapes, letters and grid rows are described in words; no picture is referred to. Drawing a line is tested by asking where lines go, how many there are, and which squares must match.

questions.skill: Interpret an equation as a multiplicative comparison
questions.stem: Look at $35 = 5 \times 7$. Which statement is true?
questions.solution: In $35 = 5 \times 7$, 35 is the product, so 35 is 5 times as many as 7. It is not 5 more than 7, since $7 + 5 = 12$.

solve.work: 35 = 5 x 7 means 35 is 5 times as many as 7. 35 is 28 more than 7, not 5; not 12 times; 7 is smaller.

questions.skill: Multiplicative comparison: find the larger amount
questions.stem: Lena has 4 stickers. Omar has 3 times as many stickers as Lena. How many stickers does Omar have?
questions.solution: "3 times as many as 4" is $3 \times 4 = 12$.

questions.skill: Choose an equation for a comparison
questions.stem: A red ribbon is 8 inches long. A blue ribbon is 4 times as long as the red ribbon. Which equation gives the length of the blue ribbon, $b$?
questions.solution: "4 times as long as 8 inches" means multiply: $b = 4 \times 8 = 32$ inches.

solve.work: 4 times as long as 8 inches: b = 4 x 8.

questions.skill: Multiplicative versus additive comparison
questions.stem: Which sentence compares by multiplying?
choices: A tower is 4 feet taller than a house.
A tower is 4 feet shorter than a house.
A tower and a house are 4 feet apart.
A tower is 4 times as tall as a house.
questions.answer: A tower is 4 times as tall as a house.
questions.solution: "4 times as tall" is a multiplicative comparison. "Taller than" and "shorter than" compare by adding or subtracting.

solve.answer: A tower is 4 times as tall as a house.
solve.work: Only "4 times as tall" is a multiplicative comparison.

solve.answer: The long rope is 2 times as long as the short rope.
solve.work: 18 = 2 x 9: the long rope is 2 times as long as the short rope.

questions.skill: Multiplicative versus additive comparison
questions.stem: Ben has 6 apples and Cara has 24 apples. Ben says Cara has 4 times as many apples. Cara says she has 18 more apples than Ben. Who is right?
choices: Both are right, using multiplication and addition.
Only Ben is right, because 24 is 4 times as many as 6.
Only Cara is right, because 24 is 18 more than 6.
Neither is right, because 24 is much more than 6.
questions.answer: Both are right, using multiplication and addition.
questions.solution: $4 \times 6 = 24$, so Cara has 4 times as many apples. Also $24 - 6 = 18$, so she has 18 more. Both comparisons are true.

solve.answer: Both are right, using multiplication and addition.
solve.work: 24 = 4 x 6 (Ben right) and 24 = 6 + 18 (Cara right): both are right.

questions.skill: Multi-step comparison problems
questions.stem: Ana scored 9 points in a game. Ben scored 4 times as many points as Ana. Cy scored 3 times as many points as Ben. How many points did Cy score?
questions.solution: Ben scored $4 \times 9 = 36$ points. Cy scored $3 \times 36 = 108$ points.

questions.skill: Choose an equation for a comparison
questions.stem: Dan has 8 toy cars. Eve has 3 times as many toy cars as Dan, and then she gets 5 more. Which expression gives the number of toy cars Eve has?
questions.solution: First Eve has 3 times as many as Dan: $3 \times 8$. Then 5 more are added: $3 \times 8 + 5 = 29$.

questions.skill: Multiplicative comparison: find the smaller amount
questions.stem: A train is 120 meters long. It is 8 times as long as a bus. How long is the bus, in meters?
questions.solution: The bus is the length that, multiplied by 8, gives 120: $120 \div 8 = 15$ meters.

questions.skill: Multiplicative comparison: find how many times as many
questions.stem: Which pair of numbers shows that the first number is 7 times the second number?
questions.solution: $56 = 7 \times 8$, so 56 is 7 times 8. In 15 and 8 the first is 7 more than the second. In 8 and 56 the order is reversed. 56 is 8 times 7.

solve.work: First = 7 x second. 56 and 8: 7 x 8 = 56, yes. 56 and 7: 56 = 8 x 7, so 8 times, not 7. 15 and 8: no. 8 and 56: first is smaller. Answer 56 and 8.

questions.skill: Multi-step comparison problems
questions.stem: Kyle is 9 years old. His grandfather is 7 times as old as Kyle. How many years older than Kyle is his grandfather?
questions.solution: The grandfather is $7 \times 9 = 63$ years old. He is $63 - 9 = 54$ years older than Kyle.

questions.skill: Choose an equation for a comparison
questions.stem: Which equation shows that 63 is 7 times as many as 9?
questions.solution: "63 is 7 times as many as 9" means 63 equals 7 multiplied by 9: $63 = 7 \times 9$.

solve.work: 63 is 7 times as many as 9: 63 = 7 x 9.

questions.skill: Multi-step comparison problems
questions.stem: Max has 24 cards, which is 3 times as many as Lia has. Lia has 4 times as many cards as Jo. How many cards does Jo have?
questions.solution: Lia has $24 \div 3 = 8$ cards. Jo has $8 \div 4 = 2$ cards.

questions.skill: Multi-step comparison problems
questions.stem: A skateboard costs 24 dollars. A scooter costs 3 times as much as the skateboard. A bike costs 25 dollars more than the scooter. How many dollars does the bike cost?
questions.solution: The scooter costs $3 \times 24 = 72$ dollars. The bike costs $72 + 25 = 97$ dollars.

questions.skill: Multi-step comparison problems

questions.solution: Owen has $5 \times 18 = 90$. Pia has $90 - 40 = 50$.

questions.skill: Multi-step comparison problems
questions.stem: Wes has 16 marbles. Xia has 3 times as many marbles as Wes. How many marbles do they have together?
questions.solution: Xia has $3 \times 16 = 48$. Together: $16 + 48 = 64$.

questions.skill: Multi-step comparison problems
questions.stem: Rob has 4 times as many cards as Sue. Sue has 14 cards. How many more cards does Rob have than Sue?
questions.solution: Rob has $4 \times 14 = 56$ cards. $56 - 14 = 42$ more.

questions.skill: Multiplicative comparison: find the smaller amount
questions.stem: A fruit stand has 7 times as many apples as pears. It has 168 apples. How many pears does it have?
questions.solution: $168 \div 7 = 24$ pears.

questions.skill: Multi-step comparison problems
questions.stem: A farmer has 6 times as many hens as ducks. He has 12 ducks. He sells 20 hens. How many hens does he have left?
questions.solution: Hens: $6 \times 12 = 72$. After selling 20: $72 - 20 = 52$.

questions.skill: Multi-step comparison problems
questions.stem: A pine tree is 15 feet tall. An oak tree is 4 times as tall as the pine tree. How many feet taller is the oak than the pine?
questions.solution: Oak: $4 \times 15 = 60$ feet. $60 - 15 = 45$ feet taller.

questions.solution: Kai has $36 \div 4 = 9$. Lou has $9 + 5 = 14$.

questions.solution: A pack holds $48 \div 6 = 8$. A case holds $3 \times 8 = 24$.

questions.skill: Multiplicative comparison: find the larger amount
questions.stem: Last month Dee earned 125 dollars. This month she earned 3 times as many dollars, and then she spent 80 dollars of this month's money. How many dollars of this month's money does she have left?
questions.solution: This month: $3 \times 125 = 375$. After spending: $375 - 80 = 295$.

questions.skill: Multiplicative versus additive comparison
questions.stem: Fern has 9 rocks. Gus has 27 rocks. Hal has 9 more rocks than Gus. Hal has how many times as many rocks as Fern?
questions.solution: Hal has $27 + 9 = 36$ rocks. $36 \div 9 = 4$ times as many.

questions.skill: Multi-step comparison problems
questions.stem: Mina has 7 pens. Ned has 4 times as many pens as Mina. Which expression gives how many more pens Ned has than Mina?
questions.solution: Ned has $4 \times 7$ pens. Subtract Mina's 7 to find how many more.

questions.skill: Multiplicative versus additive comparison
questions.stem: A ribbon is 12 inches long. A rope is 9 times as long as the ribbon. A cord is 100 inches longer than the ribbon. Which statement is true?
choices: The cord is 4 inches longer than the rope.
The rope is 4 inches longer than the cord.
The cord is 12 inches longer than the rope.
The rope and the cord are the same length.
questions.answer: The cord is 4 inches longer than the rope.
questions.solution: Rope: $9 \times 12 = 108$. Cord: $12 + 100 = 112$. The cord is 4 inches longer.

solve.answer: The cord is 4 inches longer than the rope.
solve.work: Rope 9 x 12 = 108; cord 12 + 100 = 112; cord is 4 inches longer.

questions.skill: Multiplicative comparison: find the smaller amount
questions.stem: Which problem can be solved by dividing 72 by 9?
choices: A pole is 72 feet long. A rope is 9 times as long. How long is the rope?
A rope is 72 feet long. A pole is 9 feet shorter. How long is the pole?
A rope is 72 feet long, 9 times as long as a pole. How long is the pole?
A rope is 72 feet long. A pole is 9 feet longer. How long is the pole?
questions.answer: A rope is 72 feet long, 9 times as long as a pole. How long is the pole?
questions.solution: Only the first story asks for the smaller amount when the larger is 9 times it, which is $72 \div 9 = 8$ feet. The others multiply, subtract or add.

solve.answer: A rope is 72 feet long, 9 times as long as a pole. How long is the pole?

questions.skill: Multi-step comparison problems
questions.stem: Vic has 5 times as many cards as Bo. Bo has 12 cards. Vic gives away 8 cards. Which expression shows how many cards Vic has now?
questions.solution: Vic starts with $5 \times 12$ cards and then loses 8.

questions.skill: Interpret an equation as a multiplicative comparison
questions.stem: A bus holds 60 people, a van holds 12 people and a car holds 4 people. Which statement is true?
choices: The bus holds 5 times as many as the van, and the car holds 3 times as many as the van.
The bus holds 12 times as many as the van, and the van holds 3 times as many as the car.
The bus holds 5 times as many as the van, and the van holds 3 times as many as the car.
The van holds 5 times as many as the bus, and the van holds 3 times as many as the car.
questions.answer: The bus holds 5 times as many as the van, and the van holds 3 times as many as the car.
questions.solution: $60 \div 12 = 5$ and $12 \div 4 = 3$. The larger amount is always the one that is "times as many".

solve.answer: The bus holds 5 times as many as the van, and the van holds 3 times as many as the car.

questions.solution: Seth has 8 times Tina's 125: $s = 8 \times 125$.

questions.skill: Interpret an equation as a multiplicative comparison

questions.solution: $18 \times 4 = 72$, so 72 is 4 times 18. The difference, 54, is not a "times".

questions.skill: Multiplicative versus additive comparison
questions.stem: Kai's rope is 8 feet long. Luz's rope is 4 times as long as Kai's. Mia's rope is 30 feet longer than Kai's. Whose rope is the longest?
questions.solution: Luz: $4 \times 8 = 32$ feet. Mia: $8 + 30 = 38$ feet. Mia's rope is the longest.

questions.skill: Multi-step comparison problems
